"Noor, listen to this." Hafsa tapped her psychology textbook on the kitchen table.
"Can I eat first, Hafsa Appi?"
"Old experiment. People were told they were helping test memory. Every time a stranger in the next room got an answer wrong, they pressed a switch that gave him an electric shock. Bigger each time."
"Real shocks?"
"No, he was an actor, but they didn't know that. He shouted, he banged on the wall. And a man in a grey coat just said, 'Please continue.'"
"And they stopped, obviously."
"Most didn't. Most went all the way."
Noor put her spoon down. "They must have been horrible people."
"That's what I thought. But the book says they were ordinary. Teachers, clerks. Sweating, arguing, laughing nervously, and still pressing."
"You'd never."
Hafsa was quiet. "I don't know, Noor. I do whatever the class rep says without asking. I think that's the scary part."

qa.q: What did the man in the grey coat say?
qa.a: He just said, 'Please continue.'

qa.q: Why does Hafsa go quiet when Noor says 'You'd never'?
qa.a: Hafsa feels uneasy, realising the people who kept pressing were ordinary, and since she does whatever the class rep says without asking, she might comply too.

qa.q: What choice could Hafsa practise after this realisation?
qa.a: Hafsa could start asking 'why?' before following small instructions, like the class rep's, so that saying no feels possible when it really matters.

qa.q: Why might Noor first assume the participants were horrible people?
qa.a: Hearing it for the first time, Noor finds it easier to believe only cruel people would keep pressing than to think anyone ordinary could.

grounding: Illustrates a student reading about an obedience experiment and realising ordinary, uncruel people complied, and she might too.

passage: I'm Saurabh. In second year, for a general elective, we watched grainy footage of that old obedience study: volunteers pressing switches while a hidden man cried out, a calm researcher saying, 'The experiment requires that you continue.' I sat there feeling superior. Then Chetan, next to me, whispered, 'Remember the lab file?' In first year a senior had told us to copy last year's readings instead of doing the titration, and put our own names on them. I did it in two minutes. Chetan refused and got shouted at. Watching those volunteers, I noticed none of them looked cruel. They looked polite. They looked like me. Walking back to the hostel, I told Chetan he'd been braver than I was. He just shrugged. Now, when someone senior says 'just do it', I count to three first.

qa.q: What had the senior told them to do in first year?
qa.a: To copy last year's readings instead of doing the titration, and put their own names on them.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh's feeling of superiority fade while watching?
qa.a: Saurabh noticed the volunteers didn't look cruel, only polite, and that they looked like Saurabh, who had copied the file in two minutes.

qa.q: What habit did Saurabh choose after that class?
qa.a: Now, when someone senior says 'just do it', Saurabh counts to three first before obeying.

qa.q: How might Chetan see the lab-file episode now?
qa.a: Chetan just shrugged, perhaps seeing the refusal as ordinary rather than brave, even though it cost him a shouting.

grounding: A student recalls watching an obedience study, seeing that polite, ordinary people comply, and recognising they had complied too.

Class note, third-year sociology, Tuesday. Urmila Rao.
We covered the classic obedience studies today: the switches, the actor's cries, the researcher's calm phrases. Most students reacted as usual, shocked at 'those people'. Darshan did not. He sat very still, then put his hand up: 'Ma'am, none of them sounded like villains. They kept asking "Is he all right?" and then carried on.' A few laughed. He didn't. Later he added, 'My uncle works in a shop. The owner tells him to short-weigh customers, and he does it, and he's the kindest person I know.' He looked angry, more with himself than anyone.
What I did next: I stayed back with him for ten minutes, then set the class a short writing task for Thursday: describe one small order you followed that you now doubt. I'll read them privately.

qa.q: What did the participants keep asking, according to Darshan?
qa.a: They kept asking "Is he all right?" and then carried on.

qa.q: What does Darshan's stillness and anger suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Darshan seemed shaken and angry, more with himself than anyone, realising that kind people like his uncle can obey harmful orders.

qa.q: What did Urmila choose to do with the moment, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: Urmila stayed back with Darshan and set a private writing task about one small order students now doubt, turning his insight into reflection for everyone.

qa.q: Why might the students who laughed see the study differently from Darshan?
qa.a: They still saw 'those people' as strangers unlike themselves, while Darshan had connected it to someone kind he loves.

grounding: A lecturer's note shows a student realising that ordinary, kind people obey harmful orders, and linking it to his own family.

passage:
Tuesday, library, 9 pm

Revising for the psych exam, I read the full account of that old obedience study. Ordinary men, told to give shocks to a stranger every time he got a word wrong. The stranger was an actor, but they didn't know. He yelled that his heart hurt. And a calm man in a grey coat said, "Please continue." Most of them did. All the way.

My first feeling: anger. How could they?

Then I read the notes on how they behaved. They sweated, argued, laughed nervously. They asked, "Is he all right?" None of them seemed cruel.

Walked back with Lokesh and told him. He asked, "Would you stop?" I said yes, fast. Then I remembered the canteen manager telling me to throw the leftover food in the drain instead of giving it to the boys at the gate, and I did it without a word.

I'm less sure now.
- Shankar

qa.a: He said, 'Please continue.'

qa.q: How did Shankar's feelings about the participants change as he read?
qa.a: Shankar's first feeling was anger at them, but after reading how they sweated, argued and asked if the man was all right, Shankar saw they were ordinary, not cruel.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Shankar, and what might Shankar do with it?
qa.a: Remembering throwing the food away on the canteen manager's word showed Shankar that obeying without asking comes easily, so next time Shankar might pause and question such an order.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have seen Shankar's quick 'yes'?
qa.a: Lokesh may have suspected it was too easy an answer, which is why he asked the question in the first place.

grounding: A student reading about the obedience experiments moves from anger at the participants to seeing that the student could also be the one who complies.

passage: On the bus back from Aligarh to his village, Asif, twenty, read the chapter for his psychology exam. It described an old experiment: ordinary volunteers were told by a calm man in a lab coat to give electric shocks to a stranger whenever he got an answer wrong. The shocks were fake and the stranger was an actor, but the volunteers didn't know. He cried out, begged to stop. Most volunteers kept going anyway, because the man said, "Please continue." Asif put the book down. He thought of last year, when the sarpanch told him to tear down a poor family's stall by the road, and he did, without asking why. He had told himself it wasn't his decision. His classmate Leela, beside him, asked what was wrong. "I think I'd have kept pressing the button," he said quietly.

qa.q: What did the man in the lab coat say to volunteers?
qa.a: He said, "Please continue."

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he put the book down?
qa.a: Asif felt shaken and ashamed, recognising his own obedience when he tore down the stall.

qa.q: How could Asif use this realisation in future?
qa.a: He could pause and ask why before following an order that harms someone, even from someone respected like the sarpanch.

qa.q: How might Leela respond to Asif's admission?
qa.a: Leela might be surprised but also thoughtful, perhaps wondering whether she too would have kept going.

passage: In the university library in Amman, Rania, nineteen, read about the obedience experiments for her ethics class. Ordinary people, told to give what they believed were painful shocks to a man in another room, mostly kept going, even as he shouted in pain. Not because they were cruel. Because a calm voice told them it was required. Rania felt a chill. Her friend Chidi leaned over. "I'd never do that," he said. "I'd walk out." "Would you?" Rania said. She thought of how, last semester, she'd followed her lab supervisor's instruction to throw away another student's samples to "clear space," even though she'd felt uneasy. She'd never asked him. "I didn't think I was the type either," she said. Chidi went quiet. "Okay," he said finally. "Maybe I'm not sure."

qa.a: She was reading about the obedience experiments.

qa.q: What was Rania feeling as she remembered the samples?
qa.a: Rania felt a chill of unease and guilt, realising she had obeyed without asking.

qa.q: What could Rania do next time she's told to do something that feels wrong?
qa.a: She could pause and ask the supervisor why, or check with the student affected, before acting.

Dear Sahil,
In psychology class today we read about some old experiments. Ordinary volunteers were told by a man in a lab coat to give what they believed were electric shocks to a stranger in another room. The stranger was an actor, but they didn't know that. He shouted. He begged. And most of the volunteers kept going, just because the man said, "Please continue."
I kept waiting for the part where they were cruel people. They weren't. They were teachers, clerks, people like my parents.
Then I thought about how I always say yes to my HOD, even when I disagree. I'm not sure I would have stopped.
That scares me more than the experiment.
Devika

Chaitanya and I were in the library, reading the chapter on obedience for Monday's seminar. I watched him go still over the page.
"Listen," he said, and read it aloud: most volunteers kept giving what they thought were painful shocks to a stranger who was yelling, because a researcher calmly told them to.
"They were just ordinary people," he said. "Postmen. Teachers."
I laughed. "Well, we'd never do that."
He didn't laugh. "Last month, the lab senior told us to fake the readings, and we all did."
That stopped me. I had faked mine too.
We sat there for a while. I'm Leela, and I still think about that library afternoon.

passage: Tushar, you say you'd never obey an order to hurt someone. I said that too, at twenty, in a hostel in Kharagpur. We had read about those obedience experiments in our psychology elective: volunteers giving what they thought were painful shocks because a calm man told them to continue. I was disgusted with them. That same week our hostel senior told us to make the new first-years stand in the corridor till 2 am. It seemed small. Then he said, 'Make them sing.' Then, 'Make them crawl.' I did the first two. I was halfway into the third, my own voice giving orders, when I saw a first-year's knees shaking. Something in me stopped. I said, 'No more,' walked out and knocked on the warden's door. Kamal the brave? No. Kamal who got to step three before remembering there was a choice.

qa.q: What was the senior's first order?
qa.a: Make the first-years stand in the corridor till 2 am.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel on reading about the experiments?
qa.a: Kamal felt disgusted and sure of being different from the obedient volunteers.

qa.q: Kamal said 'No more' at the third order and knocked on the warden's door. Why was that a turning point?
qa.a: It broke the chain of small steps, showing there was still a choice, and brought an adult to protect the first-years.

qa.q: What was the corridor like for the first-years?
qa.a: The first-years were frightened and humiliated, knees shaking as the orders grew worse.
